text: The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao. The name that can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name.
All in the world know the beauty of the beautiful, and in doing this they have (the idea of) what ugliness is
note: The words in round brackets are the translator's additions.

text: The highest excellence is like (that of) water. The excellence of water appears in its benefiting all things, and in its occupying, without striving (to the contrary), the low place which all men dislike.
note: The words in round brackets are the translator's additions.

text: It is better to leave a vessel unfilled, than to attempt to carry it when it is full.
When gold and jade fill the hall, their possessor cannot keep them safe.
When the work is done, and one's name is becoming distinguished, to withdraw into obscurity is the way of Heaven.
The thirty spokes unite in the one nave; but it is on the empty space (for the axle), that the use of the wheel depends.
note: The words in round brackets are the translator's additions.

text: Clay is fashioned into vessels; but it is on their empty hollowness, that their use depends.
The (state of) vacancy should be brought to the utmost degree, and that of stillness guarded with unwearying vigour.
note: The words in round brackets are the translator's additions.

text: In the highest antiquity, (the people) did not know that there were (their rulers). In the next age they loved them and praised them. In the next they feared them; in the next they despised them.
note: The words in round brackets are the translator's additions.

text: He whose (desires) are few gets them; he whose (desires) are many goes astray.
note: The words in round brackets are the translator's additions.

text: He is free from self-display, and therefore he shines; from self-assertion, and therefore he is distinguished
He who stands on his tiptoes does not stand firm; he who stretches his legs does not walk (easily).
note: The words in round brackets are the translator's additions.

text: Man takes his law from the Earth; the Earth takes its law from Heaven; Heaven takes its law from the Tao. The law of the Tao is its being what it is.
He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is intelligent. He who overcomes others is strong; he who overcomes himself is mighty.
He who is satisfied with his lot is rich
The Tao in its regular course does nothing (for the sake of doing it), and so there is nothing which it does not do.
note: The words in round brackets are the translator's additions.

text: The movement of the Tao By contraries proceeds; And weakness marks the course Of Tao's mighty deeds.
The softest thing in the world dashes against and overcomes the hardest
Who is content Needs fear no shame. Who knows to stop Incurs no blame.
There is no guilt greater than to sanction ambition; no calamity greater than to be discontented with one's lot; no fault greater than the wish to be getting.
The farther that one goes out (from himself), the less he knows.
note: The words in round brackets are the translator's additions.

text: He who devotes himself to learning (seeks) from day to day to increase (his knowledge); he who devotes himself to the Tao (seeks) from day to day to diminish (his doing).
note: The words in round brackets are the translator's additions.

text: Having arrived at this point of non-action, there is nothing which he does not do.
He who knows (the Tao) does not (care to) speak (about it); he who is (ever ready to) speak about it does not know it.
note: The words in round brackets are the translator's additions.

text: Governing a great state is like cooking small fish.
to consider what is small as great, and a few as many; and to recompense injury with kindness.
(The master of it) anticipates things that are difficult while they are easy, and does things that would become great while they are small.
note: The words in round brackets are the translator's additions.

text: The tree which fills the arms grew from the tiniest sprout; the tower of nine storeys rose from a (small) heap of earth; the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step.
note: A li is a Chinese measure of distance, about a third of a mile.

text: That whereby the rivers and seas are able to receive the homage and tribute of all the valley streams, is their skill in being lower than they
But I have three precious things which I prize and hold fast. The first is gentleness; the second is economy; and the third is shrinking from taking precedence of others.
To know and yet (think) we do not know is the highest (attainment); not to know (and yet think) we do know is a disease.
note: The words in round brackets are the translator's additions.

text: Man at his birth is supple and weak; at his death, firm and strong.
Thus it is that firmness and strength are the concomitants of death; softness and weakness, the concomitants of life.
There is nothing in the world more soft and weak than water, and yet for attacking things that are firm and strong there is nothing that can take precedence of it
Every one in the world knows that the soft overcomes the hard, and the weak the strong, but no one is able to carry it out in practice.
Sincere words are not fine; fine words are not sincere.
The sage does not accumulate (for himself). The more that he expends for others, the more does he possess of his own
note: The words in round brackets are the translator's additions.
